limits: MNIST, 2 layers, hidden 500: one dataset, one depth, one width.
Three paired seeds, no seed-variance sweep beyond that.
Layer 1 never sees the label, so this tests scale granularity, not label alignment.
Uniform groups of 10 (50 columns), 25 (20 columns) or 50 (10 columns); the per-column variant was dropped as computationally wasteful.
One dataset (MNIST) and one two-layer forward-forward architecture.
Three paired seeds, not three independent samples; intervals from them are wide.
Quantization is simulated in floating point; no integer kernels were timed.
The blockwise result shows the scale layout matters; it does not prove no other cause exists.
The aligned/unaligned pair shares a group count but not group widths, and only layer 0 is regrouped, so it isolates alignment as the cause of the gap rather than proving the whole effect.
aligned_g14 changes group count and pixel granularity at once, so it is exploratory.
The label-at-second-layer experiment changed two things at once (label position and the layer-0 objective), so it is directional evidence only.

The CIFAR-10 numbers come from two runs, one on a 20,000-example prefix of the official training order and one on the full 50,000; both use one architecture and one recipe, so they are a mechanism probe, not a benchmark. The two runs are independent trainings rather than one model resumed, so per-question flips between them are answer churn, not a quality comparison.
The layer-1 sweep cannot repeat the alignment question: layer 1 receives 500 activations, so the label columns exist only at the layer-0 input.
One of the two layer-1 runs was stopped early and is published with status running plus a RUN_STATUS.md, so it is not read as a finished result.
Nothing here extends to larger models, deeper stacks, or real language models.
